label: lemma: eta_tilde
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma: eta_tilde}
		For $u_-,u_+\geqslant0$ with $u_-+u_+>0$, $\alpha\geqslant0$ and
		$\beta>0$,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq: eta_tilde}
			\tilde\eta(u_-,u_+,\alpha,\beta)
			=
			\eta(u_+,\alpha,\beta)
			-
			\delta_-(u_-,u_+,\beta)
			\eta(u_-+u_+,\alpha,\beta).
		\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Decompose according to whether the lower boundary is reached before
		$u_+$:
		\begin{align*}
			\tilde\eta(u_-,u_+,\alpha,\beta)
			&=
			\eta(u_+,\alpha,\beta)-
			\mathbb{E}\left[
			e^{-\alpha(Y(\tau(u_+))-u_+)}
			\mathbf{1}_{\{\sigma(u_-)\leqslant\tau(u_+)\leqslant T_\beta\}}
			\right].
		\end{align*}
		On the event in the second term, $Y$ reaches $-u_-$ before $u_+$ and,
		by the strong Markov property, the process after this time is distributed
		as a fresh copy of $Y$ started from $-u_-$. Shifting the process by
		$u_-+u_+$, the remaining overshoot problem is therefore described by
		$\eta(u_-+u_+,\alpha,\beta)$. Hence
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\left[
		e^{-\alpha(Y(\tau(u_+))-u_+)}
		\mathbf{1}_{\{\sigma(u_-)\leqslant\tau(u_+)\leqslant T_\beta\}}
		\right]
		=
		\delta_-(u_-,u_+,\beta)
		\eta(u_-+u_+,\alpha,\beta),
		\]
		which proves \eqref{eq: eta_tilde}.
head: environment

label: lemma: dens and LST phase-type
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma: dens and LST phase-type}
		For $B\sim\mathbb{P}{\rm h}_d(\boldsymbol a,\boldsymbol S)$, with
		$\boldsymbol s=-\boldsymbol S\boldsymbol 1$, its density, distribution function, and LST are
		\[
		f_B(y)=\boldsymbol a^\top e^{\boldsymbol S y}\boldsymbol s,\qquad
		F_B(y)=1-\boldsymbol a^\top e^{\boldsymbol S y}\boldsymbol 1,\qquad
		\mathscr B(\alpha)=\boldsymbol a^\top(\alpha\boldsymbol I-\boldsymbol S)^{-1}\boldsymbol s,
		\]
		for $y>0$, $y\geqslant0$, and $\alpha\geqslant0$, respectively.

		{\em Throughout this section, in the derivation of the ruin probabilities we often consider the scenario `before killing', which in the case of the all-time ruin probability should be interpreted as `ever'. Specifically, we do not need a different derivation for the all-time ruin probability as the auxiliary objects introduced in Section \ref{sec: prelim} are well defined for $\beta=0$. However, since Assumption \ref{assump: distinct roots} does not always hold for $\beta=0$, the auxiliary objects can attain different forms than the ones derived in Section \ref{sec: aux for phase-type}.}

label: lemma: ruin prob v=0
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We decompose according to the first event after the process crosses the
		threshold $v=0$: either the overshoot already exceeds $u$, the process
		subsequently reaches $u$ before returning to the threshold, or it returns
		to the threshold before reaching $u$. By the strong Markov property,
		\begin{align*}
			p(u,0,\beta)
			&=
			\int_u^\infty h_1(0,y,\beta)\,\mathrm{d}y
			+\int_0^u h_1(0,y,\beta)\,
			\delta_{2,+}(y,u-y,\beta)\,\mathrm{d}y \\
			&\quad
			+\int_0^u h_1(0,y,\beta)\,
			\delta_{2,-}(y,u-y,\beta)\,\mathrm{d}y
			\,p(u,0,\beta).
		\end{align*}
		The three terms correspond, respectively, to ruin occurring directly upon
		crossing the threshold, ruin occurring before returning to the threshold,
		and returning to the threshold before ruin. Since
		\[
		0\leqslant
		\int_0^u h_1(0,y,\beta)\,
		\delta_{2,-}(y,u-y,\beta)\,\mathrm{d}y
		<1,
		\]
		we can solve for $p(u,0,\beta)$, yielding \eqref{eq: ruin prob v=0}.
head: environment

label: lemma: ruin prob v>0
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Similar to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma: ruin prob v=0}, we decompose
		according to the first event after the process crosses the threshold $v$.
		If the overshoot is at least $u-v$, ruin occurs immediately. Otherwise,
		the process either reaches $u$ before returning to $v$, or returns to $v$
		before reaching $u$. In the latter case, the strong Markov property reduces
		the problem to the one with threshold $0$ and initial surplus $u-v$.
		This yields the three terms in \eqref{eq: ruin prob v>0}.
head: environment

label: lemma: ruin prob v<0
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For this case we only need to consider two scenarios: (i) $Y_v$ crosses the level $u$ before it reaches the threshold $v$ and before killing, and (ii) $Y_v$ reaches the threshold $v$ before killing and before crossing the level $u$, at which point, by the strong Markov property, we are in a scenario which is initialized at the threshold. These two scenarios correspond to the first and second term on the right-hand side of \eqref{eq: ruin prob v<0}.

label: prop: chi(x)
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first claim, condition on the first event, which is either killing or
		hitting the threshold $v$. In terms of the free process $Y_2$,
		\begin{align*}
			\chi(x)
			&=
			e^{-\alpha x}
			\mathbb{E}\left[
			e^{-\alpha Y_2(T_\beta)}
			\mathbf{1}_{\{T_\beta<\sigma_2(x-v)\}}
			\right]
			+
			\mathbb{P}\left(\sigma_2(x-v)\leqslant T_\beta\right)\chi(v).
		\end{align*}
		By \eqref{eq: sigma before killing} and the strong Markov
		property we have that
		$
		\mathbb{P}\left(\sigma_2(x-v)\leqslant T_\beta\right)
		=e^{-\psi_2(\beta)(x-v)},
		$
		while
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\left(e^{-\alpha Y_2(T_\beta)}\right)
		=
		\frac{\beta}{\beta-\varphi_2(\alpha)}.
		\]
		Hence,
		\begin{align*}
			\chi(x)
			&=
			e^{-\alpha x}
			\frac{\beta}{\beta-\varphi_2(\alpha)}
			-
			e^{-\alpha v}
			\frac{\beta}{\beta-\varphi_2(\alpha)}
			e^{-\psi_2(\beta)(x-v)}
			+
			e^{-\psi_2(\beta)(x-v)}\chi(v),
		\end{align*}
		which gives \eqref{eq: chi(x) for x > v}.
		
		For the second claim, conditioning on the first event for $Y_1$ (which is either reaching $0$, exceeding $v$, or being killed)
		\begin{equation*}
			\chi(x)
			=
			\delta_{1,-}(x,v-x)\chi(0)
			+
			\int_0^\infty
			\tilde h_1(x,v-x,y,\beta)\chi(v+y)\,\mathrm{d}y
			+
			\delta_{1,\star}(x,v-x).
		\end{equation*}
		Substituting \eqref{eq: chi(x) for x > v} into the integral gives
		\begin{align*}
			\int_0^\infty
			\tilde h_1(x,v-x,y,\beta)\chi(v+y)\,\mathrm{d}y
			&=
			\frac{\beta}{\beta-\varphi_2(\alpha)}
			e^{-\alpha v}
			\left(
			\tilde{\eta}_1(x,v-x,\alpha,\beta)
			-
			\tilde{\eta}_1(x,v-x,\psi_2(\beta),\beta)
			\right)
			\\
			&\quad
			+
			\tilde{\eta}_1(x,v-x,\psi_2(\beta),\beta)\chi(v),
		\end{align*}
		and \eqref{eq: chi(x) for x < v} follows.

label: prop: chi(x) capacity
title: Proposition
head: environment
labels: eq: chi(x) capacity v < x < K

title: Proof
body_md:
We start with the first claim. For $v < x \leqslant K$, conditioning on the first event, which is either killing, hitting $v$, or hitting $K$, and applying the strong Markov property yields \eqref{eq: chi(x) capacity v < x < K}.
		
		For the second claim, for $0 < x \leqslant v$, conditioning on the first event and applying the strong Markov property gives
		\begin{align*}
			\notag\widehat\chi(x) &= \delta_{1,-}(x, v-x, \beta)\widehat\chi(0) + \int_0^{K-v} \tilde{h}_1(x,v-x,y,\beta)\widehat\chi(v+y)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
			&\:\:\:\:\:+ \int_{K-v}^\infty \tilde{h}_1(x,v-x,y,\beta)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\widehat\chi(K) + \delta_{1,\star}(x, v-x, \beta).
		\end{align*}
		Substituting \eqref{eq: chi(x) capacity v < x < K} into the first integral yields
		\begin{align*}
			\int_0^{K-v}  \tilde{h}_1(x,v-x,y,\beta)\widehat\chi(v+y)\,\mathrm{d}y 
			=\:& \int_0^{K-v} \tilde{h}_1(x,v-x,y,\beta)\delta_{2,-}(y,(K-v)-y,\beta)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\widehat\chi(v) \:+\\
			& \int_0^{K-v} \tilde{h}_1(x,v-x,y,\beta)\delta_{2,+}(y,(K-v)-y,\beta)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\widehat\chi(K)\:+ \\
			& \int_0^{K-v} \tilde{h}_1(x,v-x,y,\beta)\delta_{2,\star}(y,(K-v)-y,\beta)\,\mathrm{d}y,
		\end{align*}
		which yields \eqref{eq: chi(x) capacity 0 < x < v}.

label: eq: p^V for 0<=u<=v and x=0
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $x=0$, conditioning on the first arrival and on whether killing occurs before it gives
		\begin{align*}
			p^V(u,v,0,\beta) &= \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1 + 
				\beta}\Bigg(\int_{(u,\infty)}\mathbb{P}(B_1\in\mathrm{d}y) + \int_{[0,u]}\mathbb{P}(B_1 \in \mathrm{d}y)\,\delta_{1,+}(y,u-y,\beta) \\
			&\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\: + \int_{[0,u]}\mathbb{P}(B_1 \in \mathrm{d}y)\,\delta_{1,-}(y,u-y,\beta)\,p^V(u,v,0,\beta)\Bigg).
		\end{align*}
		Rearranging yields \eqref{eq: p^V for 0<=u<=v and x=0}.
		For $0<x\leqslant u$, either $u$ is crossed before the workload reaches zero or the system empties first, in which case the process restarts from $0$. This immediately yields \eqref{eq: p^V for 0<=u<=v and 0<x<=v}.
head: environment

label: eq: p^V for u>v and v<x<u
title: Lemma
head: environment
labels: eq: p^V for u>v and v<x<u

title: Proof
body_md:
In the decomposition of the ruin probabilities, we use the hitting times of the levels
		$0$ and $v$ as regenerative points.
		
		For the first claim, condition on whether the workload process crosses $u$ before reaching $v$
		and before killing, or reaches $v$ first. This directly gives the two terms on the
		right-hand side of \eqref{eq: p^V for u>v and v<x<u}: the first corresponds to
		crossing $u$ before reaching $v$ or being killed, while the second corresponds to
		reaching $v$ first and subsequently crossing $u$ starting from $v$.
		
		For the second claim, starting from $0<x\leqslant v$, we distinguish the possible regenerative events.
		The first term on the right-hand side of
		\eqref{eq: p^V for u>v and 0<x<=v} corresponds to crossing $v$ with an overshoot
		large enough to cross $u$ as well. The second corresponds to crossing $v$ with a
		smaller overshoot and subsequently crossing $u$ before returning to $v$ or being
		killed. The third term covers the case where $v$ is reached again before $u$ is
		crossed or the process is killed. Finally, the fourth term corresponds to reaching
		$0$ before crossing $v$ or being killed.

label: lemma:B invertible
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\boldsymbol{Bt}=0$ for some $\boldsymbol{t}\in\mathbb{C}^d$. This implies that
		\begin{equation*}
			0 = \sum_{j=1}^d t_j\mathscr{B}_j(\alpha_k) = \sum_{j=1}^d t_j\frac{q_j(\alpha_k)}{p(\alpha_k)} = \frac{\boldsymbol{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{q}(\alpha_k)}{p(\alpha_k)}.
		\end{equation*}
		Because none of the $\alpha_k$ is an eigenvalue of $\boldsymbol{S}$, $p(\alpha_k) \neq 0$. Hence $\boldsymbol{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{q}(\alpha_k) = 0$ for all $k\in[d]$. 
		
		Recall that each $q_j(\alpha)$ is at most of degree $d-1$, hence $\boldsymbol{t}^\top\boldsymbol{q}(\alpha)$ is at most of degree $d-1$. Since the $\alpha_k$ are distinct we thus have $\boldsymbol{t}^\top\boldsymbol{q}(\alpha)\equiv0$.
		
		It follows that $(\boldsymbol{t}^\top\boldsymbol{q}(\alpha)) / p(\alpha) = 0$
		for all $\alpha$ that are not an eigenvalue of $\boldsymbol{S}$. Since
		\[
		\frac{\boldsymbol{q}(\alpha)}{p(\alpha)} = \left(\alpha\boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{S}\right)^{-1}\boldsymbol{s}
		= \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\boldsymbol{S}^m\boldsymbol{s}}{\alpha^{m+1}}
		\]
		for sufficiently large $\alpha$, we obtain
		\[
		\boldsymbol{t}^\top\boldsymbol{S}^m\boldsymbol{s}=0
		\quad \text{for all} \quad m\geqslant0.
		\]
		For a minimal phase-type representation, the vectors
		$\boldsymbol{s},\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{s},\ldots,\boldsymbol{S}^{d-1}\boldsymbol{s}$ span $\mathbb{R}^d$, see e.g. \cite[Theorem 4.2.16]{BN}, so we must have $\boldsymbol{t}=0$. Thus $\boldsymbol{B}$ is nonsingular.
head: environment

label: lemma: q vs Bc
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq: q_j = Bc
title: Proof
body_md:
We will show that the entries of the two sides of
		\eqref{eq: q vs Bc} are the same polynomials. To this end, let
		$j\in[d]$ be given. For the corresponding entry on the right-hand
		side of \eqref{eq: q vs Bc} we have 
		\begin{equation}\label{eq: q_j = Bc}
			\sum_{k=1}^{d}\boldsymbol{B}_{jk}^\top\mathfrak{C}_k(\alpha) = \sum_{k=1}^{d} \frac{q_j(\alpha_k)}{p(\alpha_k)} \cdot (-r)c_k (\alpha_k-\alpha_{d+1}) \prod_{\ell=1, \ell\neq k}^{d} (\alpha - \alpha_\ell).
		\end{equation}
		First note that \eqref{eq: q_j = Bc} is a polynomial in $\alpha$ of
		degree at most $d-1$. We will show that this polynomial agrees with
		$q_j(\alpha)$ at the $d$ points $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d$. Let
		$n\in[d]$. Evaluating \eqref{eq: q_j = Bc} at $\alpha=\alpha_n$ gives
		\begin{equation}\label{eq: rho_n in}
			\sum_{k=1}^{d} \frac{q_j(\alpha_k)}{p(\alpha_k)} \cdot (-r)c_k (\alpha_k-\alpha_{d+1}) \prod_{\ell=1, \ell\neq k}^{d} (\alpha_n - \alpha_\ell).
		\end{equation}
		For every $k\in[d]$, except $k=n$, the term within the summation is
		zero, so \eqref{eq: rho_n in} reduces to
		\begin{equation}\label{eq: rho_n in 2}
			\frac{q_j(\alpha_n)}{p(\alpha_n)} \cdot (-r)c_n
			\prod_{\ell=1, \ell\neq n}^{d+1} (\alpha_n - \alpha_\ell)
			= q_j(\alpha_n),
		\end{equation}
		by \eqref{eq: def c_k}. Hence the two polynomials agree at
		$\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d$ and are therefore identical. Since this
		holds for all $j\in[d]$, \eqref{eq: q vs Bc} follows.
